clue.text: Made a lot of the effect of the Higgs boson

definitions.text: the effect of the Higgs boson

blocks.note: first meaning: manufactured in great quantities on a production line

blocks.clueFragment: the effect of the Higgs boson
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: the particle is what gives other particles their weight

explanation.surface: A physicist boasting of how much was made of the Higgs boson discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: Physicists say the Higgs field is what gives particles mass, so its effect is that mass is produced; 'Made a lot of' also reads as 'made a fuss about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods turned out in huge numbers by factory methods are described with this compound adjective.

clue.text: Scoundrel entering address for woman that’s seen on the way

indicators.note: one thing entering another goes inside it, so the rogue word is placed within the form of address

blocks.note: ma'am, the short polite way to address a lady
an old word for a rotter

explanation.surface: A rogue sidling up to a woman he greets politely in the street.
explanation.definitionFit: This crushed-stone surfacing, named after John McAdam, is laid on roads, so it is seen on the way.

clue.text: Left-leaning politician upsetting stoical comrade

indicators.note: upsetting means overturning, knocking the following words out of their order

explanation.surface: A centre-left politician annoying a phlegmatic fellow party member.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of this moderate party tradition sit on the centre-left of the political spectrum.

clue.text: Gathering fuel around loch

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the fuel wraps about the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for loch on maps

explanation.surface: Collecting fuel from around a Scottish lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A fold of cloth stitched in place is a gathering in dressmaking terms.

clue.text: Line on graph an editor amended

indicators.note: something amended has been altered, so the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: An editor has corrected a line on a chart.
explanation.definitionFit: The vertical coordinate, measured along the y-axis, is the mathematical term for this graph line.

clue.text: Royal Navy invested in unserviceable vessels

indicators.note: to be invested in is to be clothed in, so the navy sits inside the other abbreviation

blocks.note: U/S is the abbreviation for unserviceable

explanation.surface: The navy has put money into ships that are no longer fit for service.
explanation.walkthrough: The naval surface makes vessels look like ships; they are pots.
explanation.definitionFit: Large vases or containers for ashes are vessels in the sense of receptacles.

clue.text: This helps viewers look at what starts auction running

blocks.note: to eye is to look at
lot one, with the Roman numeral, is the first item sold

explanation.surface: A tip on how to watch the opening of a sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Auctions begin with Lot 1, written here with I for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Viewers here are eyes, and a soothing liquid for sore eyes helps them.

clue.text: Ascetic who was looked up to with remarkable solemnity in places

definitions.text: Ascetic who was looked up to

indicators.note: remarkable suggests something extraordinary, out of its ordinary form, so the next word is rearranged
in tells us the rearranged word goes inside the word for locations

explanation.surface: A revered holy man, treated with notable gravity wherever he went.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters sit inside the word for places, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This fifth-century Syrian saint lived for decades atop a pillar, so people literally had to raise their eyes to him.

clue.text: Cheeky, dismissing National Trust support for rambler, perhaps

indicators.note: dismissing means sending away, so the heritage body's abbreviation is removed from the adjective

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for the heritage charity

explanation.surface: A walker cheekily brushing off the National Trust, which owns much of the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust is the British charity that looks after historic houses and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: An inner sole cushions the foot inside a walking boot, so it supports a hiker.

clue.text: Chapter’s long to store in memory for quick recall

definitions.text: store in memory for quick recall

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
to ache for is to long for

explanation.surface: Someone longing to memorise a chapter so they can quote it.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing, this is a small fast store holding recently used data so it can be retrieved quickly.

clue.text: Plant a new food shop in London’s East End

indicators.note: on a map east is right, and in written English the right-hand end of a word is its end
in places the shop and its preceding letters inside the selected letters

blocks.note: the last three letters of the city's name, its eastern end
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Opening a new delicatessen in the East End of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is London's eastern district; read on the page, a word's east end is its last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This yellow-flowered weed with a puffball seed head is a common plant.

clue.text: Impressing daughter, progressing down-river

explanation.surface: A daughter shows off her skill on a river trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressing' looks like making a good impression; it means pressing men into service.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress sailors or soldiers was to conscript them, which is what calling people up for service does.

clue.text: Spanish dance or English ball must be given backing

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the three preceding words are read right to left

blocks.note: a high ball in tennis or cricket

explanation.surface: A choice between a Spanish dance and an English ball, which needs sponsors.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively Spanish dance in triple time, made famous by Ravel, is a classic of the genre.

clue.text: No excessive way to gain speed

explanation.surface: Advice that there is no extreme method for picking up pace.
explanation.definitionFit: Something kept within reasonable limits is not extreme, the plain opposite of excessive.

clue.text: Standard rule about private rooms

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the verb for ruling goes round the rooms

explanation.surface: A normal regulation covering personal living quarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as an adjective meaning normal; it is a flag. The Red Ensign is the flag flown by British merchant ships.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag, and this red flag with the Union Jack in its corner is flown by British merchant ships.

clue.text: One getting married taking note of money matters

indicators.note: taking here means taking away, removing the abbreviation from the money word

blocks.note: n. is the abbreviation for note, as in a footnote reference

explanation.surface: A groom-to-be paying attention to the household budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking note' looks like paying attention; here taking means removing.
explanation.definitionFit: A man engaged to be wed is one who is about to get married.

clue.text: Skilful design for portico

explanation.surface: An expert architectural plan for a porch.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical architecture this is a porch whose columns stand only across the front of a building.

clue.text: Bashful about medical film like Doctor in the House

definitions.text: film like Doctor in the House

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shy word goes round the medical abbreviation

explanation.surface: A shy student in a medical film.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor in the House is a 1954 British film about medical students, a light-hearted romp.
explanation.definitionFit: That 1950s picture about hospital trainees is a humorous film, an example of the genre.

clue.text: Be concerned about a fine decanter

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the worry verb goes round the two following pieces

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Worrying about a precious glass decanter.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass jug for serving wine or water at table is a kind of decanter.

clue.text: Hyperactive fencer is injured with it

indicators.note: something injured is damaged and out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An overexcited swordsman has been hurt by his own weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild, frantic, excessively energetic activity is described by this adjective, a close synonym.

clue.text: Acclaimed Conservative youth securing politics degree

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the young man holds the degree inside him

blocks.note: Philosophy, Politics and Economics, the Oxford degree

explanation.surface: A young Tory praised for getting his Oxford degree.
explanation.walkthrough: PPE is the Oxford course taken by many British politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience that applauds someone has greeted them with acclaim, so the verb fits.

clue.text: Describing losing time in sport

indicators.note: losing means doing without, so the abbreviation for the time unit is dropped

blocks.note: to describe a circle is to trace its outline

explanation.surface: Commentary on time-wasting in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Describe is used in its geometry sense, drawing a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Competing in speed contests, with horses, cars or on foot, is a sport.

clue.text: Might a musical instrument be given a Spanish name?

blocks.clueFragment: Might a musical instrument be given a Spanish name?
blocks.note: surface: wondering whether an instrument could be called something in Spanish
setter's reading: put the question 'is a percussion instrument a…?' and run the words together into a girl's name

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an instrument could be named in Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as IS A BELL A, the name reads like a question about whether a bell is a musical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: This name, borne by the queen who sponsored Columbus, is a classic Spanish girl's name.

clue.text: Suit was effective, securing European female

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the past-tense verb holds the two abbreviations inside it

explanation.surface: A smart outfit worked well, keeping a European woman safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like clothing; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To be fitting or appropriate for someone is to suit them, as in 'it ill becomes you'.

clue.text: Sort of leather without name

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the leather sits round the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A type of leather sold without a brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, an old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A sort or type of something is a variety, so the noun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Father needs ease of movement for this quality of eggshell

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for a priest

explanation.surface: A dad needs a nimble touch when handling eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggshell breaks easily, so its defining property is delicacy or breakability.

clue.text: Camera setting is just dandy when covering street

indicators.note: covering means lying over or around, so the dandy wraps the road abbreviation

blocks.note: a dandy is a fop; just means merely

explanation.surface: A photographer finds the settings fine for shooting street scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just dandy' reads as 'perfectly fine'; dandy alone is a well-dressed man.
explanation.definitionFit: This number marks the aperture on a camera lens, one of its basic settings.

clue.text: Completely out of puff?

blocks.note: surface: utterly exhausted and short of breath
setter's reading: a puff is a promotional blurb, so this describes something never promoted at all

explanation.walkthrough: Puff looks like breath; it is the old word for a boastful advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Something never promoted in the papers or on posters has had no publicity at all.
